pair.title: The correction, and what it would be on a plane
pair.mini: A level line of sight over flat ground and over a globe. On a plane the ground stays under it and a surveyor's staff needs no correction. On a globe the ground falls away by d²/2R, and every sight is corrected for it.
pair.text: The same level line of sight, over a plane and over a globe. On a plane the ground stays directly under the line, and a surveyor's staff reads the true height difference with no correction at all. On a globe the ground falls away from the line by d²/2R, so every sight carries a curvature correction, together with one for refraction. Surveyors do not assume the curve: their instruments keep finding it, and national survey manuals tabulate the correction [1]. Curvature is exaggerated in the drawing.
pair.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: long level sights that need no curvature correction to close.
drop.title: Two numbers that are not the same
drop.mini: From one end of a line, the ground falls away below the horizontal by d²/2R. A chord stretched between the two ends stands above the ground only in the middle, by d²/8R. Two different numbers for two different questions.
drop.text: Two quantities are easily confused. From one end of a line, the ground falls away below that end's horizontal by d²/2R over a distance d. A straight chord stretched between the two ends of the line stands above the ground only in the middle, by d²/8R, four times less. The first matters for a level sight from one end; the second for a straight beam or tunnel between two points. Engineers building long straight structures work with both. The drawing is schematic.
drop.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: long straight structures that sit flush on level ground end to end.
level.title: Levelling: the correction applied a thousand times a day
level.mini: Geodetic levelling uses short, balanced sights of 60 m. There the curvature correction is only 0.3 mm per sight, and with equal back and fore sights it cancels exactly. The whole procedure is designed around the curve.
level.text: Standard geodetic levelling, as the U.S. manual prescribes it [1]: sights of about 60 m, balanced so that the back-sight and the fore-sight are the same length. At 60 m the curvature correction is a mere 0.3 mm per sight, and because the two distances are equal it cancels exactly between the two staff readings, along with most of the refraction. The procedure is designed around the curve: short sights, balanced setups, thousands of times per line. On a flat Earth none of that discipline would buy anything.
level.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: long unbalanced levelling sights that close without a curvature correction.
excess.title: A triangle on a sphere has more than 180°
excess.mini: On a plane a triangle's angles sum to exactly 180°. On a sphere they sum to more, by the triangle's area divided by R²: about one arcsecond per 197 km². Surveyors budget for it, triangle by triangle.
excess.text: On a plane, a triangle's three angles add to exactly 180°, always. On a sphere they add to more, by the spherical excess, equal to the triangle's area divided by the radius squared: about one arcsecond for every 197 km² on the Earth. Surveyors do not debate this; they budget for it, triangle by triangle. Gauss's great triangle Brocken–Hohehagen–Inselsberg, measured in his Hanover survey in the 1820s, had an excess of about 14.85″, dozens of times the resolution of his theodolite [1]. The drawing is schematic.
excess.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: large surveyed triangles whose angles sum to exactly 180°.
tri.title: Triangulation: the angles confess
tri.mini: A documented survey triangle on a turning globe. Its three angles add up to more than 180°, and the excess matches the area over R². {{mcase}}
tri.text: A documented survey triangle, the network named above the text, drawn on a turning globe as an equilateral triangle. On a sphere the three angles add to more than 180° by the area divided by R². {{case}} On a plane the excess would be zero.
tri.case-gauss: For Gauss's triangle Brocken–Hohehagen–Inselsberg of 1823, sides 69, 85 and 107 km, drawn as the equilateral triangle of the same area (side {{side}} km), which carries the same excess: each angle is {{ang}}° and the sum exceeds 180° by {{exc}}; Gauss measured 14.85″ [1]. The area law and the theodolite agree to a hundredth of an arcsecond.
tri.case-real: For {{name}}, sides of about {{side}} km, the area law gives each angle {{ang}}° and an excess of {{exc}} per triangle.
tri.case-illus: For an illustrative continental triangle, sides of {{side}} km and no real network, each angle is {{ang}}° and the excess reaches {{exc}}.
tri.mcase-gauss: For Gauss's triangle of 1823 the law gives {{exc}}; he measured 14.85″.
tri.mcase-real: For {{name}}, sides of about {{side}} km, the law gives {{exc}} per triangle.
tri.mcase-illus: For an illustrative 1,000 km triangle the excess reaches {{exc}}.
tri.net-struve: a typical triangle of the Struve chain
tri.net-osgb: a typical primary triangle of the OSGB retriangulation
tri.net-gts: a typical long-sided triangle of the Great Trigonometrical Survey
tri.net-cassini: a typical triangle of Cassini's Paris meridian
tri.net-spain: the Spain–Algeria junction of 1879, Mulhacén side

tri.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: large survey triangles with no spherical excess.
radius.title: The Earth's radius from 32 pairs of theodolite readings
radius.mini: Thirty-two pairs of reciprocal zenith angles, 18 to 157 km long, from U.S. surveys of 1900 and 1977. Uncorrected they give about 7,150 km, the refraction-enlarged radius. Corrected with k = 0.13, the median lands within a few percent of 6,371 km.
radius.text: When two stations sight each other at the same moment, the two zenith angles add up to 180° plus (1 − k)·d/R, so the excess over 180° gives the radius. Thirty-two pairs are on file: seven lines of 70 to 93 km surveyed from Mount Livermore, Texas, in 1977 [1], and twenty-five from the transcontinental triangulation of 1900, spanning 18 to 157 km [2]. Uncorrected, they cluster near 7,150 km, about 12% high; that excess is refraction, the effective radius R/(1 − k). Applying the standard coefficient k = 0.13 [3] brings the median within a few percent of 6,371 km. A plane needs the sum to be exactly 180°, which puts R at infinity.
radius.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: reciprocal zenith angles summing to exactly 180°, giving an infinite radius.
angles.title: Sixteen hundred triangles: the curvature from their angles
angles.mini: The angles of {{n}} survey triangles in the United States, France, Russia, Britain and at the Cape, read in the surveyors' own tables. Their sums exceed 180° in proportion to the area, as on a sphere of radius {{R}} km; a plane allows no excess at all.
angles.text: The three angles of each triangle as observed at the stations, in our own transcription of five surveys: the U.S. Coast Survey's arcs (Schott, 1900 and 1902) [1][2], Delambre and Méchain's meridian, Maclear's Cape arc, Roy's Greenwich–Paris chain and Struve's arc [4], every row checked against the printed sums, logarithms and sines. On a sphere the angles add up to 180° plus the area divided by R² [3]; on a plane, to exactly 180°. The areas are carried from measured base lines with the observed angles alone, so no radius goes into the data. The excess grows with the area, up to 75″ for a 14,500 km² triangle between peaks in Utah and Nevada, and the line through zero gives R = {{R}} km ({{lo}} to {{hi}}). On the globe every side lies as measured; on the flat map centred on the North Pole, at its one best scale, north–south sides come out about {{np}} % short and east–west sides at the Cape more than twice too long.
angles.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: angle sums that stay at 180° whatever the size of the triangle.
